name: Panic disorder
dsmPointer: See DSM-5-TR: Anxiety Disorders — Panic Disorder
summary: Built on a feedback loop: the client notices a body change, reads it as a sign of disaster (breathlessness as suffocation, dizziness as collapse), and the fear amplifies the sensations until the episode peaks. Because some attacks arrive without warning, the client starts monitoring the body and arranging life around preventing the next one, and those protective habits keep the loop going. Many first present to primary or emergency care. Consider medical and substance-related causes before treating the picture as a primary anxiety condition. For clinician review only; this is not a diagnosis.

durationGate.note: Date the first attack, then ask how long the client has been bracing for the next one or changing plans because of it. Confirm the exact timing requirement in DSM-5-TR.

ruleOuts.label: Hyperthyroidism
ruleOuts.note: Can produce palpitations, tremor, heat intolerance and anxiety. Consider thyroid testing through the client's medical provider.

ruleOuts.label: Cardiac arrhythmia or other heart disease
ruleOuts.note: Chest pain, palpitations and breathlessness need medical evaluation first, especially with exertional symptoms, fainting, age or cardiac risk factors.

ruleOuts.label: Asthma or COPD
ruleOuts.note: Breathlessness and air hunger may reflect a respiratory condition or its treatment (e.g., beta-agonist inhalers).

ruleOuts.label: Hypoglycemia
ruleOuts.note: Shakiness, sweating and dread linked to missed meals or diabetes treatment suggest checking blood glucose patterns.

ruleOuts.label: Vestibular, seizure or rare endocrine causes
ruleOuts.note: Episodic dizziness, stereotyped spells or paroxysmal hypertension (e.g., pheochromocytoma) warrant medical work-up.

ruleOuts.label: Caffeine, stimulants or decongestants
ruleOuts.note: High caffeine intake, energy drinks, prescribed or illicit stimulants and some cold medicines can trigger panic-like episodes.

ruleOuts.label: Alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal
ruleOuts.note: Rebound anxiety, tremor and sweating after cutting down can mimic panic and may be medically dangerous; refer for medical assessment.

ruleOuts.label: Cannabis or other substance effects
ruleOuts.note: Acute intoxication or withdrawal from several substances can provoke attacks. This app does not store substance-use information.

ruleOuts.label: Attacks better explained by another mental health condition
ruleOuts.note: Attacks that only ever arrive with one kind of trigger are cued rather than unexpected. Trace the trigger (see the differentials list), and consider obsessional and separation-related fears as well.

specifiers.label: Nocturnal panic (descriptive)
specifiers.note: Attacks that wake the person from sleep. Ask about them directly and consider sleep-related differentials such as sleep apnea or reflux.

specifiers.label: Limited-symptom attacks (descriptive)
specifiers.note: Episodes with fewer bodily sensations than a full attack. Track them, since they often keep avoidance going.

specifiers.label: Co-occurring agoraphobia
specifiers.note: DSM-5-TR assesses and codes agoraphobia separately. ICD-10-CM also offers F40.01 (agoraphobia with panic disorder) and lists panic disorder with agoraphobia under that code. Confirm which convention your setting and payer use.

differentials.label: Social anxiety disorder (ICD-10-CM title: Social phobia, unspecified)
differentials.distinguishing: Attacks occur mainly in social or performance settings, and the core fear is being judged or embarrassed rather than the attack itself.

differentials.label: Specific phobia, situational type (ICD-10-CM title: Other situational type phobia)
differentials.distinguishing: Attacks are limited to one narrow trigger (e.g., flying, driving, heights) rather than also arising unexpectedly.

differentials.label: Illness anxiety disorder (ICD-10-CM title: Hypochondriasis)
differentials.distinguishing: Health fear is constant rather than coming in spikes; the client checks, researches and seeks reassurance between visits.

differentials.label: Anxiety disorder due to another medical condition (ICD-10-CM title: Anxiety disorder due to known physiological condition)
differentials.distinguishing: A medical illness, such as thyroid, heart or lung disease, is producing the episodes through its effects on the body; they rise and fall with that illness.

differentials.label: Generalized anxiety disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Chronic, diffuse worry and tension rather than abrupt, time-limited surges. The two often co-occur.

differentials.label: Posttraumatic stress disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Attacks set off by trauma reminders, together with re-experiencing and avoidance of reminders, point toward PTSD.

comorbidities.label: Agoraphobia
comorbidities.note: Many clients start avoiding places after repeated attacks, fearing they will be stranded with symptoms. Assess both; they are now separate diagnoses.

comorbidities.label: Major depressive disorder
comorbidities.note: Depression commonly follows or accompanies panic disorder, and their combination is linked to more impairment. Screen for low mood and ask directly about suicidal thoughts.

comorbidities.label: Posttraumatic stress disorder
comorbidities.note: Panic attacks are frequent in PTSD. Ask about trauma history when attacks cluster around reminders.

comorbidities.label: Generalized anxiety disorder
comorbidities.note: Broad everyday worry can coexist with panic attacks; treatment plans can address both.

comorbidities.label: Alcohol or sedative use to cope
comorbidities.note: Some clients use alcohol or sedatives to dampen attacks. Screen gently and refer as needed. This app does not store or transmit substance-use information.

interventions.name: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for panic disorder
interventions.evidence: NICE CG113 (2011; 2020 surveillance kept the recommendations): CBT is a recommended first-line psychological treatment for panic disorder. APA Division 12 has listed CBT for panic with strong research support; its page notes re-evaluation, so check the current rating.
interventions.note: Usually includes psychoeducation about the panic cycle, interoceptive exposure, in-vivo exposure and restructuring of catastrophic misreadings of body sensations.

interventions.name: Interoceptive exposure
interventions.evidence: Core component of CBT protocols for panic (see NICE CG113; APA Division 12 CBT listing).
interventions.note: Deliberately brings on feared sensations (e.g., spinning, breathing through a straw). Get medical clearance first for cardiac, respiratory, seizure or vestibular conditions, pregnancy, or other medical concerns.

interventions.name: CBT-based self-help (guided or unguided)
interventions.evidence: NICE CG113 lists self-help based on CBT principles as a lower-intensity option within stepped care.
interventions.note: Useful while waiting for therapy or for milder presentations; review progress regularly.

interventions.name: Applied relaxation
interventions.evidence: APA Division 12 has listed applied relaxation for panic with modest research support (verify the current rating).
interventions.note: Second-line or adjunctive option. Some clients feel more anxious when they first relax; prepare them for this.

interventions.name: Referral for medication evaluation
interventions.evidence: NICE CG113 names an SSRI as the first-line medication for panic disorder and advises against benzodiazepines for this condition.
interventions.note: Refer to psychiatry, a primary care provider or a psychiatric nurse practitioner. Prescribing decisions rest with the prescriber.

culturalNotes: Some Latino clients, particularly of Caribbean background, may describe an 'ataque de nervios'. It often erupts after a family shock or conflict and tends to be more emotionally expressive than a typical panic attack, so the two overlap only in part. Ask what happened just before and what the episode means to the client and family.

Some Cambodian clients may describe 'khyal cap' (wind attacks), understood within a traditional model of wind rising in the body and threatening serious harm. Bodily alarm is read through that framework, so explore the client's own explanation and feared consequences before reframing symptoms.

Many clients first describe panic in purely physical terms (heart, stomach, 'nerves'). Respect the bodily explanation, coordinate with medical care, and introduce the panic cycle as an added way of understanding, not a replacement.
Use a trained professional interpreter, not family members, when assessing in a language other than English; idioms for fear and bodily alarm translate poorly.
GAD-7 scores do not measure panic severity directly, and cut-offs may perform differently across languages and cultural groups. Interpret scores alongside the interview.

If a client draws on faith or spiritual practices to cope with attacks, explore this respectfully. Use spiritual or faith-integrated approaches only when the client asks for them and after informed consent (see the AACC Code of Ethics for faith-based counselors).

requiredFeatures.note: Attacks that come without warning are not documented; this pattern needs at least some of them (see DSM-5-TR). Clarify whether the attacks are unexpected or happen only in set situations.

redFlagRules.message: Manic or hypomanic signs are documented in this input. Screen for bipolar disorder (ICD-10-CM F31.x) and refer for psychiatric evaluation before treatment planning.
Psychotic symptoms are documented in this input and are not part of this pattern. Consider a psychotic disorder, substance effects or a medical cause, and refer for an urgent psychiatric evaluation.
